questions.q: True or False: The opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. In rectangle ABCD, with AB as transversal, ∠A + ∠B = 90° + 90° = 180°. These are internal angles on the same side of the transversal, so AD ∥ BC. The same argument gives AB ∥ DC.
s: Reason: the internal angles on the same side of a transversal add up to 180°, so the sides are parallel

questions.q: The diagonals AC and BD of a quadrilateral ABCD are both 20 cm long, they bisect each other at O, and ∠AOB = 100°. (a) What kind of quadrilateral is ABCD? (b) Find ∠OAB. (c) Find ∠OAD. (d) Use (b) and (c) to find ∠BAD.
questions.a: (a) A rectangle, because its diagonals are equal and bisect each other. (b) OA = OB, so ∠OAB = (180° − 100°) ÷ 2 = 40°. (c) ∠AOD = 180° − 100° = 80° and OA = OD, so ∠OAD = (180° − 80°) ÷ 2 = 50°. (d) ∠BAD = 40° + 50° = 90°, as it must be in a rectangle.
s: (a) Rectangle, with the reason (equal diagonals that bisect each other)

questions.q: A carpenter must make a rectangular frame ABCD by pinning two wooden strips together and running a thread round their four ends. He has one strip 60 cm long and another 56 cm long, and he may saw a strip shorter but cannot make one longer. (a) If he pins the two strips at their midpoints without sawing, will the thread form a rectangle? Give the reason. (b) Which strip should he saw, and by how much? (c) Where should he then put the pin on each strip? (d) In the finished frame AB = 50 cm. Find CD and name the property used. (e) Use the angles at A and B to explain why AD ∥ BC.
questions.a: (a) No. The diagonals of a rectangle are equal, but these strips are 60 cm and 56 cm, so the frame cannot be a rectangle even though the strips bisect each other. (b) He must saw the 60 cm strip, since the 56 cm strip cannot be lengthened: cut off 60 − 56 = 4 cm so that both strips are 56 cm. (c) At the midpoint of each strip, 28 cm from each end, so that the equal diagonals bisect each other. (d) CD = 50 cm, because the opposite sides of a rectangle are equal. (e) ∠A = ∠B = 90°, so ∠A + ∠B = 180°. AB is a transversal to AD and BC, and when the interior angles on the same side of a transversal add up to 180°, the lines are parallel, so AD ∥ BC.
s: (a) No: the diagonals of a rectangle must be equal, and 60 cm ≠ 56 cm
(b) Saw 4 cm off the 60 cm strip
(c) Pin each strip at its midpoint, 28 cm from each end
(d) CD = 50 cm, opposite sides of a rectangle are equal
(e) ∠A + ∠B = 180° on the same side of transversal AB, so AD ∥ BC

questions.q: Class 8 students in a Pune school test the Carpenter's method. Each group pins two 40 cm strips at their midpoints, sets them at a different angle, runs a thread round the four ends A, B, C, D, and measures the four corners with a protractor. Group A (strips at 40°) records 90°, 91°, 90°, 89°. Group B (strips at 75°) records 89°, 90°, 91°, 90°. Group C (strips at 120°) records 90°, 90°, 90°, 90°. The teacher asks whether these readings prove that the method always gives a rectangle. (a) Groups A and B read 91° and 89° at two corners. Should they decide that their frames are not rectangles? Give a reason. (b) Do the readings of the three groups prove that the method works for every angle? Give a reason. (c) Let the angle between the strips be x, with ∠AOB = x where O is the pin. Write ∠OAB and ∠OAD in terms of x. (d) Hence show that ∠DAB = 90° for every x, and say what this adds to the readings.
questions.a: (a) No. Their strips are equal and pinned at the midpoints, so the diagonals are equal and bisect each other, which makes a rectangle; a difference of 1° in a protractor reading is a measuring error (the readings still add up to 360°). (b) No. Measuring a few frames only gives a conjecture: we cannot be sure that a frame at some other angle will also give 90° corners. (c) OA = OB, so ∠OAB = (180° − x) ÷ 2 = 90° − x/2. ∠AOD = 180° − x and OA = OD, so ∠OAD = x ÷ 2 = x/2. (d) ∠DAB = (90° − x/2) + x/2 = 90° for every value of x. This proves the result for all angles, so it is certain and no longer only a conjecture.
s: (a) No: equal diagonals bisecting each other give a rectangle; 89° and 91° are measuring errors
(b) No: the readings give only a conjecture, not a proof for every angle
(d) ∠DAB = 90° for every x, which proves the result

In square PQRS the diagonals PR and QS meet at O, and PR = 10 cm. (a) Find QS. (b) Find ∠POQ. (c) Name the congruence condition that shows ∆POQ ≅ ∆ROQ, and the three pairs of equal parts.
questions.a: (a) The diagonals of a square are equal, so QS = 10 cm. (b) The diagonals of a square bisect each other at 90°, so ∠POQ = 90°. (c) SSS: OP = OR (the diagonals bisect each other), PQ = RQ (the sides of a square are equal) and OQ is common.
s: (c) SSS, with OP = OR, PQ = RQ and OQ common

questions.q: Answer each part about squares in one step. (a) Is every square a rectangle? Give the reason from the definitions. (b) Is every rectangle a square? Give an example with side lengths. (c) In a Venn diagram of rectangles and squares, where is the curve for squares drawn? (d) Leela wants to construct a square with one diagonal 7 cm. How long must the other diagonal be, and where must the two diagonals cross each other? (e) At what angle must the two diagonals cross?
questions.a: (a) Yes. A rectangle is a quadrilateral with all angles 90°, and every square has all angles 90°. (b) No. A rectangle 6 cm long and 3 cm wide has all angles 90°, but its sides are not all equal, so it is not a square. (c) Inside the curve for rectangles, since every square is a rectangle. (d) The other diagonal must also be 7 cm, and the two diagonals must cross at their midpoints (bisect each other). (e) At 90°.
s: (a) Yes, a square has all angles 90°
(b) No, with an example such as a 6 cm by 3 cm rectangle
(d) Other diagonal 7 cm, crossing at the midpoints

questions.q: A tiler cuts two four-sided tiles and must decide which one is a square. Tile 1 has all four sides 15 cm and both diagonals 21.2 cm. Tile 2 has all four sides 15 cm and diagonals of 24 cm and 18 cm, which cross at right angles. The diagonals of both tiles bisect each other. (a) What type of quadrilateral are both tiles, judging by their sides alone? (b) Using its diagonals, show that Tile 1 is a rectangle. (c) Hence decide what Tile 1 is, with the reason. (d) A helper says, 'The diagonals of Tile 2 bisect each other at right angles, so Tile 2 is a square.' What condition on the diagonals is the helper leaving out? (e) Is Tile 2 a square? Say what it is.
questions.a: (a) A rhombus, because all four sides are equal (15 cm). (b) The diagonals of Tile 1 are equal (21.2 cm each) and bisect each other, and a quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other is a rectangle. (c) Tile 1 is a rectangle with all four sides equal, so it is a square. (d) For a square the diagonals must be equal in length as well as bisect each other at 90°. (e) No. Its diagonals are 24 cm and 18 cm, which are unequal, so it is not a rectangle and not a square; it is a rhombus that is not a square.
s: (a) Rhombus, since all four sides are 15 cm
(b) Equal diagonals that bisect each other make Tile 1 a rectangle
(c) A rectangle with all sides equal, so a square
(d) The diagonals must also be equal
(e) No: diagonals 24 cm and 18 cm are unequal, so Tile 2 is a rhombus that is not a square

Three angles of a quadrilateral are 80°, 95° and 110°. Find the fourth angle.
questions.a: The four angles add up to 360°. The three given angles add up to 80° + 95° + 110° = 285°, so the fourth angle is 360° − 285° = 75°.

questions.q: True or False: A quadrilateral can have three angles of 90° and a fourth angle of 80°. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°. Three right angles use up 270°, so the fourth angle must be 360° − 270° = 90°, not 80°.
s: Reason: the angle sum is 360°, so the fourth angle is forced to be 90°

questions.q: In quadrilateral PQRS, ∠P = 70°, ∠Q = 110° and ∠R is twice ∠S. (a) Find ∠R + ∠S. (b) Find ∠S. (c) Find ∠R. (d) Which pair of sides of PQRS must be parallel, and why? (e) Can PQRS be a parallelogram? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) ∠R + ∠S = 360° − (70° + 110°) = 180°. (b) 2∠S + ∠S = 180°, so ∠S = 60°. (c) ∠R = 120°. (d) With PQ as transversal, ∠P + ∠Q = 70° + 110° = 180°, so PS ∥ QR. (e) No. In a parallelogram the opposite angles are equal, but ∠P = 70° and ∠R = 120°; also ∠Q + ∠R = 230°, so PQ is not parallel to SR.
s: (d) PS ∥ QR, because ∠P + ∠Q = 180° on the same side of transversal PQ

questions.q: A school is building a four-sided stage ABCD. For the carpet to fit, every corner of the stage must be at least 70° and at most 120°. The builder fixes ∠B = 95° and wants ∠C and ∠D to be equal. In the first plan ∠A = 105°. (a) Find ∠C + ∠D in the first plan. (b) Find ∠C and ∠D, and say whether the first plan follows the carpet rule. (c) The principal wants ∠A as large as possible. If ∠C and ∠D are both made 70°, the smallest allowed, what would ∠A be? (d) Can that plan be used? Find the largest ∠A that keeps every corner within the rule, and the values of ∠C and ∠D then.
questions.a: (a) The angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360°, so ∠C + ∠D = 360° − (105° + 95°) = 160°. (b) ∠C = ∠D = 160° ÷ 2 = 80°. All four corners (105°, 95°, 80°, 80°) lie between 70° and 120°, so the plan follows the rule. (c) ∠A = 360° − (95° + 70° + 70°) = 125°. (d) No: 125° is more than the 120° allowed. The largest ∠A is 120°; then ∠C + ∠D = 360° − (120° + 95°) = 145°, so ∠C = ∠D = 72.5°, which is at least 70°, so every corner keeps to the rule.

questions.q: The diagonals AC and BD of parallelogram ABCD meet at O, with AC = 12 cm and BD = 9 cm. (a) Find OA. (b) Find OB. (c) Are the diagonals equal? Say what this shows.

questions.q: Ravi draws parallelogram ABCD with ∠DAB = 50° and says, 'Then ∠ABC is also 50°, because the angles of a parallelogram are equal.' (a) Is he right? Give a reason. (b) Find ∠ABC. (c) Find ∠BCD and ∠CDA.
questions.a: (a) No. Only the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal; the adjacent angles add up to 180°. (b) ∠ABC = 180° − 50° = 130°. (c) ∠BCD = ∠DAB = 50° and ∠CDA = ∠ABC = 130°.
s: (a) Says he is wrong: adjacent angles add up to 180°, only opposite angles are equal

questions.q: In parallelogram ABCD, AB = (3x − 4) cm, CD = (x + 8) cm, AD = (2y + 1) cm and BC = (y + 6) cm. Also ∠A = (4z + 10)° and ∠B = (2z + 20)°. (a) Find x and the length of AB. (b) Find y and the length of AD. (c) Find the lengths of BC and CD. (d) Find z. (e) Find all four angles of ABCD.

Farmer Dev's field PQRS is a parallelogram. Two irrigation pipes run along its diagonals: PR is 40 m long, QS is 30 m long, and they cross at O. He measures ∠PQR = 118°. He plans to put one sprinkler at O and wants to know how far its spray must reach to wet all four corners, and whether his field is a rectangle. (a) Find PO and QO, naming the property used. (b) Find ∠QRS and ∠RSP. (c) Is the field a rectangle? Give two reasons. (d) What is the shortest spray reach from O that wets all four corners? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so PO = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 m and QO = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 m. (b) Adjacent angles add up to 180°, so ∠QRS = 180° − 118° = 62°; opposite angles are equal, so ∠RSP = ∠PQR = 118°. (c) No: the diagonals are unequal (40 m and 30 m), and ∠PQR = 118°, not 90°. (d) 20 m. O is 20 m from P and R but only 15 m from Q and S, because the diagonals bisect each other but are unequal, so the spray must reach the farther pair of corners.
s: (a) PO = 20 m and QO = 15 m, as the diagonals bisect each other
(c) Not a rectangle: unequal diagonals and an angle that is not 90°
(d) 20 m, the distance from O to P and R

questions.a: (a) The diagonal bisects the angle at D, so ∠ADC = 2 × 25° = 50°. (b) Adjacent angles add up to 180°, so ∠DAB = 180° − 50° = 130°. (c) ∠BCD = ∠DAB = 130°, and the diagonal AC bisects it, so ∠ACB = 65°.

questions.q: Two strips AC and BD cross at right angles at O so that OA = OC and OB = OD, and a thread is run round A, B, C and D. (a) Show that ABCD is a rhombus. (b) If ∠OAB = 32°, find ∠OBA. (c) Find ∠BAD and ∠ABC. (d) Find ∠BCD and ∠CDA, naming the property used. (e) Find ∠DCA, and use it with ∠BAC to show that AB ∥ DC.
questions.a: (a) The four triangles AOB, COB, COD and AOD each have a right angle at O and equal sides around it, so they are congruent by SAS. Hence AB = CB = CD = DA, and ABCD is a rhombus. (b) ∠OBA = 180° − 90° − 32° = 58°. (c) The diagonal AC bisects ∠BAD, so ∠BAD = 2 × 32° = 64°, and the diagonal BD bisects ∠ABC, so ∠ABC = 2 × 58° = 116°. (d) The opposite angles of a rhombus are equal, so ∠BCD = ∠BAD = 64° and ∠CDA = ∠ABC = 116°. (e) The diagonal AC bisects ∠BCD, so ∠DCA = 64° ÷ 2 = 32°. Then ∠BAC = ∠DCA = 32°; these are alternate angles made by the transversal AC with AB and DC, so AB ∥ DC.
s: (a) The four right-angled triangles are congruent by SAS, so all four sides are equal
(e) ∠DCA = 32° = ∠BAC, equal alternate angles, so AB ∥ DC

The side face of a wooden step is an isosceles trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC and AD = BC. If ∠D = 72°, find ∠C and ∠A.
questions.a: In an isosceles trapezium the angles opposite to the equal sides are equal, so ∠C = ∠D = 72°. AD is a transversal to the parallel sides AB and DC, so ∠A + ∠D = 180° and ∠A = 180° − 72° = 108°.

questions.q: True or False: In kite ABCD, with AB = BC and CD = DA, the diagonal BD is perpendicular to the diagonal AC. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. Triangles ABD and CBD are congruent by SSS, so BD bisects ∠ABC. Then triangles AOB and COB are congruent by SAS, so ∠AOB = ∠COB. These two angles add up to 180°, so each is 90°.
s: Reason: triangles AOB and COB are congruent, so ∠AOB = ∠COB and each is 90°

questions.q: Kite ABCD has AB = BC and CD = DA, and its diagonals meet at O. ∠ABO = 38°. Find (a) ∠CBO, (b) ∠AOB, (c) ∠BAO.
questions.a: (a) The diagonal BD bisects ∠ABC, so ∠CBO = ∠ABO = 38°. (b) The diagonals of a kite are perpendicular, so ∠AOB = 90°. (c) In triangle AOB, ∠BAO = 180° − 90° − 38° = 52°.

questions.q: Two cardboard copies of an isosceles triangle with sides 9 cm, 9 cm and 5 cm are joined edge to edge, along sides of the same length, to make a quadrilateral. (a) They are joined along their 5 cm sides. Name the quadrilateral and give its four side lengths. (b) They are joined along a 9 cm side so that the two 5 cm sides meet at a corner. Name the quadrilateral, with the reason. (c) They are joined along a 9 cm side so that the two 5 cm sides are opposite each other. Name the quadrilateral, with the reason. (d) In the quadrilateral of (b), the joined 9 cm side is one diagonal. What does it do to the other diagonal?
questions.a: (a) A rhombus: its four sides are 9 cm, 9 cm, 9 cm and 9 cm. (b) A kite: going round, the sides are 9 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm and 9 cm, so it can be labelled ABCD with AB = BC = 5 cm and CD = DA = 9 cm. (c) A parallelogram: the sides in order are 9 cm, 5 cm, 9 cm and 5 cm, so the opposite sides are equal, and the two copies lie the opposite way round, so the alternate angles at the joined side are equal and the opposite sides are parallel. (d) It bisects the other diagonal and is perpendicular to it.
s: (b) Kite, two pairs of equal adjacent sides (5, 5 and 9, 9)
(c) Parallelogram, opposite sides equal and parallel
(d) Bisects the other diagonal at right angles

questions.q: Kite ABCD has AB = BC and CD = DA, with ∠ABC = 80° and ∠ADC = 50°. (a) Show that ∠BAD = ∠BCD, naming the congruent triangles and the condition used. (b) Find ∠BAD. (c) The diagonal BD bisects ∠ABC. Find ∠ABD. (d) Find ∠ADB, and check that the angles of triangle ABD add up to 180°. (e) Mira says, 'This kite is also a trapezium.' Is she right? Give a reason using the angles.
questions.a: (a) In ∆ABD and ∆CBD, AB = CB, AD = CD and BD is common, so ∆ABD ≅ ∆CBD by SSS, and ∠BAD = ∠BCD as corresponding parts. (b) The angles add up to 360°, so ∠BAD + ∠BCD = 360° − 80° − 50° = 230° and ∠BAD = 115°. (c) ∠ABD = 80° ÷ 2 = 40°. (d) BD also bisects ∠ADC, so ∠ADB = 50° ÷ 2 = 25°; check: 115° + 40° + 25° = 180°. (e) No. For a pair of opposite sides to be parallel, the two angles at the ends of a side joining them must add up to 180°. Here ∠A + ∠B = ∠B + ∠C = 195° and ∠C + ∠D = ∠D + ∠A = 165°, so no pair of sides is parallel and it is not a trapezium.
s: (e) No: no two adjacent angles add up to 180° (195° and 165°), so no sides are parallel

questions.q: A school garden club lays out a flower bed PQRS. The back edge PQ and the front edge SR are parallel, with PQ = 4 m and SR = 7 m, and the two side edges PS and QR are both 3 m. The gardener notes that ∠P is twice ∠S. The club secretary says, 'The two side edges are equal, so the bed is a parallelogram, and the fence for the back edge can be cut the same length as the front edge.' (a) What type of quadrilateral is the bed? Give the reason. (b) Find ∠S and ∠P. (c) Find ∠R and ∠Q, and use the angles to decide whether the bed can be a parallelogram. (d) Is the secretary's fencing plan right? Explain where her reasoning goes wrong.
questions.a: (a) An isosceles trapezium: one pair of opposite sides is parallel (PQ ∥ SR) and the non-parallel sides are equal (PS = QR = 3 m). (b) PS is a transversal to the parallel sides, so ∠P + ∠S = 180°. With ∠P = 2∠S, 3∠S = 180°, so ∠S = 60° and ∠P = 120°. (c) The angles opposite to the equal sides are equal, so ∠R = ∠S = 60° and ∠Q = ∠P = 120°. In a parallelogram the opposite angles are equal, but ∠P = 120° and ∠R = 60°, so the bed is not a parallelogram. (d) No. The back edge is 4 m and the front edge is 7 m, so a 7 m fence would not fit. Her mistake is that equal side edges do not make a parallelogram: a parallelogram needs both pairs of opposite sides parallel, and an isosceles trapezium has equal non-parallel sides with only one pair parallel.
s: (a) Isosceles trapezium: PQ ∥ SR and PS = QR
(c) ∠R = 60°, ∠Q = 120°; opposite angles unequal, so not a parallelogram
(d) No: PQ = 4 m, not 7 m; equal non-parallel sides do not make a parallelogram
